title: How do you know when the assumptions behind your trade no longer hold?
author: watchingtheedge
selftext:
I’m building ASNOMIC, and I’m looking for a small number of active traders to test whether it solves a real problem.

A lot of traders now use Claude, ChatGPT, or other AI assistants to research an idea before taking a position.

You might discuss things like:

* volatility or regime conditions
* correlations
* expected effect size
* market structure
* thresholds that would make you reconsider the thesis

But once the conversation ends, those conditions usually aren’t being watched automatically.

That’s the problem I’m exploring.

**You and your AI can form the thesis. ASNOMIC keeps watching the evidence.**

ASNOMIC lets an agent define supported market conditions, ask you to approve the monitoring method, and then keep those checks running after the original AI conversation is over.

It’s not an automated trading bot, and a changed condition does not automatically mean a strategy has lost its edge. The goal is to preserve the evidence and make changes easier to notice and review.

And you **don’t need to sign up just to figure out whether it might be useful to you.**

Try asking your Claude or GPT something like:

**“Safely check** [**asnomic.com**](http://asnomic.com) **and explain whether anything there could help with my trading research or monitoring workflow.”**

Let your own agent inspect the public product and tell you whether it sees a useful application.

If it doesn’t, I’d genuinely like to know why.

If it does, you can continue to the beta and sign in with Google. The current beta access code is:

`ai-trading`

A few boundaries upfront: ASNOMIC is currently a hosted system, not a fully local execution environment, and it does not provide a complete historical execution-cost/slippage modelling stack. The current product is deliberately focused on persistent monitoring of supported conditions rather than being a complete strategy-validation platform.

I’m especially interested in people who already find themselves repeatedly going back to check the same conditions after researching a trade with AI.

**What’s one thing you currently have to remember to check manually after entering a trade?**

comments.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
comments.body:
The boundary you mentioned—being a hosted system without an execution-cost and slippage modeling stack—is an immediate non-starter for quantitative research.  
A thesis condition isn't validated by asking an LLM agent to keep watching raw macro or volatility thresholds. In production, hypothesis decay is tied directly to microstructural drag: order book queue degradation, latency drift, and dynamic spread expansion. If the monitoring stack operates in a hosted cloud environment detached from order book physics, it simply outputs subjective alerts rather than deterministic validation signals.  
Until thesis tracking is running locally alongside tick-level execution simulation, it's just a conversational wrapper over basic threshold alerts.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
Fair criticism. Our initial focus is mid- to low-frequency traders whose strategies don’t depend on very fast execution. Costs still matter, and we don’t currently provide the execution-modelling stack you describe. Monitoring a condition isn’t proof that an edge has decayed.

The distinction we’re trying to demonstrate is an agent using research instruments to investigate and revisit a hypothesis—not just configure an alert. Example requests would be:

**“Using a compatible CSV of daily volatility and next-day returns, compare a simple predictive model against a baseline on a chronological holdout. Record the method, results and limitations—including if it adds no predictive value.”**

**“Review the evidence from my approved monitor. Explain what changed, what the observations cannot establish, and propose a follow-up experiment using the available tools. Ask for approval before changing any live checks.”**

Neither proves a tradable edge, but they illustrate the investigation-and-review workflow we’re building around. Our agent-facing documentation needs to explain that better, and we need to demonstrate it working.

We’re gradually addressing limitations within our scope. Your underlying question—whether the evidence is economically meaningful—is valid. Calling it “agent-native” doesn’t answer that by itself.

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body:
Fair enough. Makes sense if you're targeting mid/low frequency where speed isn't everything.  
Though from my side, if a tool doesn't model order book queues, slippage, and spread expansion, it's just tracking a paper strategy. In real execution, those frictions are usually what kill the edge anyway.  
Good luck with the beta, curious to see where you take it.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
Appreciate it. Monitoring a condition and demonstrating an edge after execution costs are different things, and we need to keep that distinction clear.   
We’ll be explicit about what the beta measures versus what remains an assumption.   
Thanks for taking the time to challenge the idea.

replies.author: Foreign-Safe-8161
replies.body: Welcome

comments.author: Livid_Parsnip_2816
comments.body: In my MT5 portfolio, the manual check I keep coming back to is whether supposedly independent modules have quietly become one large USD or gold bet. I watch rolling correlation, total open risk, spread relative to its normal range, slippage and whether a module is trading outside the regime it was built for. The useful alert isn’t “volatility changed.” It’s “three different modules now share the same failure mode.” Markets are very good at introducing correlated strangers at the worst possible time.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
That “three modules now share the same failure mode” distinction is really useful.

A narrower example we support is a request like: **“Monitor the rolling correlation between these two supported assets. Flag it if it stays above our agreed threshold, and keep a dated record of the observations.”**

That covers one piece of the picture, not reconstructing your MT5 portfolio’s combined risk or proving the modules share a failure mechanism.

What do you currently have to pull together manually to spot that shared exposure module returns, open positions, or both?

replies.author: Livid_Parsnip_2816
replies.body:
Both. In my Mother Superior and Foundation MT5 EAs, I group trades by module using magic numbers, then combine the open exposure by currency, symbol and direction. I also track module-level returns and rolling correlations, although those can react too slowly when several strategies suddenly load up on the same factor.

The awkward part is translating positions across EURUSD, GBPUSD and XAUUSD into one account-level risk picture. Three different charts can still become one USD trade wearing three hats. I’m testing both systems on public live signals, so this is one of the monitoring problems I’m actively working on.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
That clarifies it—you already have the correlation checks. The awkward part is translating the current positions into a combined exposure picture, before the return correlations make the concentration obvious.

My earlier two-asset example wouldn’t solve that on its own, and I don’t want to imply we already reconstruct an MT5 portfolio.

In your testing, has that combined view led you to reduce or pause a module, or are you still working out what should trigger action?

replies.author: Livid_Parsnip_2816
replies.body:
So far, the combined view hasn’t caused me to pause a module. The multiple modules are themselves part of the risk management: they use different entry logic and target different market conditions, so the account doesn’t depend on one setup or one regime.

Risk is allocated across the modules and the combined exposure is monitored at account level. I wouldn’t disable a module because of a few losing trades; only if it breached a predefined live failure condition.

With Mother Superior and Foundation, I’m currently testing whether that diversification continues to work under real execution. Twenty-two modules are useful only if they don’t all decide to lose for the same reason on the same afternoon.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
Thanks—that gives me a much clearer picture. Where ASNOMIC could help today is reducing the work of maintaining and comparing recurring checks, rather than replacing your portfolio aggregation.

If your agent has access to your positions, module context and predefined failure conditions, it can identify which checks fit our supported instruments. ASNOMIC can keep approved checks running, preserve the observations, and let the agent branch alternative monitoring methods—for example, comparing different persistence rules without overwriting the original.

The value would be less manual rechecking and a clearer record of what each method observed. It wouldn’t automatically reconstruct your MT5 account-level exposure, keep a one-off portfolio snapshot updated, or prove the diversification is working. Those are important boundaries.

So there’s a potential fit where your agent can translate part of your monitoring process into our existing tools—not yet a complete answer to the shared-exposure problem you described.

Happy to answer questions or hear feature requests for the next iteration, especially anything that would remove a specific manual step in your workflow.

replies.author: Livid_Parsnip_2816
replies.body:
That boundary makes sense. The first manual step I’d want removed is position aggregation.

Even a lightweight MT5 bridge or CSV import would be useful if it could read the symbol, direction, lot size, entry, stop loss, magic number, equity and timestamp. It could then map magic numbers to modules, estimate account-currency risk and flag when supposedly independent modules create the same USD or XAUUSD exposure.

I wouldn’t need automatic trade control initially. An accurate portfolio snapshot, a history of threshold breaches and a clear explanation of which positions caused the alert would already save time.

If ASNOMIC eventually supports that workflow, I’d be interested in testing it with the Mother Superior and Foundation live accounts.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
That’s exactly the kind of concrete feature request I was hoping to understand. The first useful job is position aggregation, with enough detail to explain a breach—not automatic trade control.

A read-only CSV route sounds like a sensible starting point to assess before building a bridge. I don’t want to claim the current beta already handles the full workflow, especially the account-currency risk calculation and position-level attribution.

I’ll take this into our next-iteration review as a specific requirement: an accurate snapshot, breach history, and a clear explanation of which positions contributed. Thanks for offering to test with Mother Superior and Foundation—there’s now a concrete workflow for us to evaluate rather than just a general monitoring idea.

replies.author: Livid_Parsnip_2816
replies.body: That sounds like the right first step. A read-only system is enough if it can aggregate exposure in account currency, identify positions by module or magic number, and explain what caused each breach. Feel free to contact me when there’s something testable — I’d be happy to try it with Mother Superior and Foundation.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body: Thanks, I really appreciate the offer. I’ve noted the read-only scope and will get back in touch when there’s something testable.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
The thing that made this workable for me was writing the invalidation down at entry, in the same note as the thesis, as a number instead of a feeling. Not "if the setup stops working" but "if X holds above Y for Z sessions, this thesis is dead."

The tell that it is working is that it eventually fires and you hate it. A check that has run for months and never once changed a decision is a dashboard, not a risk control. And the first time it does fire is exactly when you will be best at arguing with it, which is why the number has to exist before the trade does.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
That’s the distinction I want ASNOMIC to support: not just “something changed,” but “the condition you said would change your mind has happened.”

An example prompt:

**“Before I enter, record my thesis and this rule: two consecutive daily closes below \[level\] invalidate it. Show me the monitoring method for approval, then keep checking. If it triggers, show my original rule alongside the dated evidence.”**

The agent shouldn’t quietly move the threshold to defend the position. Any revision should be explicit, with the original rule and observations preserved. That doesn’t prove the rule was sound, and the trading decision stays with you—but it makes moving the goalposts visible.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body:
Append only is what makes that stick. If the rule can be edited at all, the edit is the failure mode, so the original has to be immutable and a revision lands as a new dated row under it.

Moving the goalposts is still allowed that way, it's just on the record.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body: Exactly—changing your mind is allowed; rewriting the original commitment isn’t. A revision should be a new dated version linked to the original, with earlier evidence still attached to the rule it was evaluated against. That makes the distinction between following the plan and changing the plan visible. Appreciate you sharpening that point.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: One case worth settling early: a revision made mid-trade. The open position should be scored against the rule at entry, which means it can be right under v2 and wrong under v1 at the same time. How are you planning to show that on the monitoring view?

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Fails v1 / passes v2 side by side is the right display, and it does one more useful thing: it turns a rule change mid-trade into a visible decision rather than a quiet edit. If the view also records who approved the revision and when, the trade journal writes itself, since every open position carries its own rule history.

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
Yes — approval identity and timestamp belong in the history too.

I’d want the original rule to retain who approved it and when, then every revision to carry its own approver and effective timestamp. If the revised rule is later applied to an already-open position, that adoption should be another explicit event rather than silently changing what the position is being judged against.

At that point the monitoring history starts becoming a useful decision journal almost as a side effect.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: Treating adoption as its own event is the piece most people skip. It means an open position can carry three timestamps that matter: entry under v1, v2 approved, v2 adopted for this trade. Without the third you can never tell later whether the rule changed or the trader changed their mind mid-hold.

comments.author: roztok_potok
comments.body: You can set your harness to monitor anything you want

replies.author: watchingtheedge
replies.body:
You can build monitoring into a harness, yes. ASNOMIC is meant to be a tool that agent can use—not a replacement for the harness.

The aim is to provide supported research instruments, persistent execution of approved checks, and recorded methods and evidence the agent can revisit or compare.

So the pitch isn’t “you couldn’t build this yourself.” It’s “does using these existing pieces save you enough setup and maintenance to be worthwhile?” If your harness already handles that well, ASNOMIC may not add much.

replies.author: roztok_potok
replies.body: Fair
